claims.claim: The N-terminal residues of the ClpP protomer proximal to the X5 ClpX protomer are held rigidly through contacts with the ATPase.
claims.source: In contrast, the N-terminal residues of the ClpP protomer proximal to the X5 ClpX protomer, are held rigidly through contacts with the ATPase (Figure 2G right).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The interaction between the X5 protomer and ClpP N-terminal gate is mediated by a pair of α-helices from protomer X5 (residues 254–262 and 291–296) adjacent to the IGF loop, and by another X5 α-helix that precedes the pore-2 loop (residues 186–192).
claims.source: This interaction is mediated by a pair of α-helices from protomer X5 (residues 254–262 and 291–296) adjacent to the IGF loop, and by another X5 α-helix that precedes the pore-2 loop (residues 186–192).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claims.claim: The three α-helices from X5 stabilize the β-hairpin structure of the ClpP N-terminal residues by interacting with Arg17 at the top of the hairpin.
claims.source: The three α-helices stabilize the β-hairpin structure of the ClpP N-terminal residues by interacting with Arg17 at the top of the hairpin (Figure 2E inset).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The interactions between X5 and ClpP gates are unique for the X5 protomer due to the lateral displacement of the ClpX ring relative to the axial pore of ClpP.
claims.source: These interactions are unique for the X5 protomer due to the lateral displacement of the ClpX ring relative to the axial pore of ClpP (Figure 2A), with the X2 protomer shifted furthest from the pore while the X5 protomer is pulled overtop of the pore (Figure 2D and F).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figures 2A, 2D, and 2F.

claims.claim: Gate rigidification appears to be mediated by an allosteric effect when IGF loops engage their respective ClpP binding pockets, akin to the effect observed upon ADEP binding.
claims.source: Gate rigidification therefore appears to be mediated by an allosteric effect when IGF loops engage their respective ClpP binding pockets, akin to the effect observed upon ADEP binding (Gersch et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gates are rigidified even without direct contact with ClpX, and is compared to ADEP binding.

claims.claim: In the ClpXP complex with substrate bound, only a single ClpX protomer (X5) interacts directly with a single ClpP gate at any given time.
claims.source: In the ClpXP complex with substrate bound, only a single ClpX protomer (X5) interacts directly with a single ClpP gate at any given time.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claims.claim: The mechanism of substrate translocation involves movement of the ClpX ring on the apical surface of ClpP, with each ClpX protomer forming contacts with a ClpP gate as translocation proceeds.
claims.source: The mechanism of substrate translocation described below involves movement of the ClpX ring on the apical surface of ClpP, with each ClpX protomer forming contacts with a ClpP gate as translocation proceeds.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: ClpX fits into the emerging consensus for how AAA+ unfoldases engage substrate.
claims.source: ClpX fits neatly into the emerging consensus for how AAA+ unfoldases engage substrate (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated by comparing ClpX to other AAA+ unfoldases with citations.

claims.claim: In both Conformations A and B, five of the six pore-1 loops of ClpX interact tightly with the substrate backbone, with Tyr153 forming the majority of the interface.
claims.source: In both Conformations A and B, five of the six pore-1 loops of ClpX interact tightly with the substrate backbone, with Tyr153 forming the majority of the interface (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Five protomers generate a right-handed spiral that wraps around an 8 to 10 residue stretch of the substrate along the central channel of ClpX.
claims.source: These protomers generate a right-handed spiral that wraps around an 8 to 10 residue stretch of the substrate along the central channel of ClpX (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: In Conformation A, the X1 pore-1 loop in the US orientation is disengaged.
claims.source: In Conformation A, the X1 pore-1 loop in the US orientation is disengaged, with the X2 protomer at the top of the spiral.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, the X6 pore-1 loop is disengaged (LS orientation), while the X1 pore-1 loop engages a new section of substrate.
claims.source: In Conformation B, the X6 pore-1 loop is disengaged (LS orientation), while the X1 pore-1 loop engages a new section of substrate (Figure 3D) and the X5 protomer is now located closest to the ClpP surface.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: When transitioning between substrate-engaged and disengaged states, the X6 pore-1 loop undergoes a large conformational change.
claims.source: When transitioning between substrate-engaged and disengaged states, the X6 pore-1 loop undergoes a large conformational change (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: As the X6 pore-1 loop disengages the substrate, the 'lasso' fold that allows Tyr153 and Val154 to point toward the substrate is replaced by a short α-helix immediately following the GYVG motif of the loop.
claims.source: As it disengages the substrate the 'lasso' fold (Figure 3E, left) that allows Tyr153 and Val154 of pore-1 to point toward the substrate is replaced by a short α-helix immediately following the GYVG motif of the loop.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, the X1 and X5 protomers make additional contacts with the substrate.
claims.source: Interestingly, the X1 and X5 protomers make additional contacts with the substrate in Conformation B.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, the X1 protomer extends its pore-2 loop residues Ile198 and Thr199 to engage the substrate at a position three or four residues down the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds.
claims.source: Whereas all of the pore-2 loops from the other five protomers are radially removed and disengaged from the substrate, the X1 protomer extends its pore-2 loop residues Ile198 and Thr199 to engage the substrate at a position three or four residues down the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds (Figure 3D and F).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and F.

claims.claim: The RKH loops are conserved motifs among the ClpX family of AAA+ unfoldases and are known to contribute to substrate recognition.
claims.source: The RKH loops, located at the top of the ClpX ring (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), are conserved motifs among the ClpX family of AAA+ unfoldases and are known to contribute to substrate recognition (Martin et al., 2007; Farrell et al., 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, only the RKH loop of X5 directly engages substrate, with its His230 residue interacting at a position three or four residues up the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds.
claims.source: In Conformation B, only the RKH loop of X5 directly engages substrate, with its His230 residue interacting at a position three or four residues up the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds (Figure 3D and F).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and F.

claims.claim: In order to contact substrate, the RKH loop of the X5 protomer rearranges to point toward ClpP, in contrast to the other RKH loops that point away from the axial channel of ClpX.
claims.source: In order to contact substrate at this position the RKH loop of the X5 protomer rearranges to point toward ClpP (Figure 3F), in contrast to the other RKH loops that point away from the axial channel of ClpX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The five RKH loops not contacting substrate are located away from the substrate and have weaker density in the maps, likely indicating flexibility.
claims.source: These five RKH loops are located away from the substrate, and have weaker density in the maps, likely indicating flexibility.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps and interpreted as flexibility.

claims.claim: The cryo-EM maps allowed unambiguous identification of the nucleotide bound to each ClpX protomer.
claims.source: The cryo-EM maps allowed unambiguous identification of the nucleotide bound to each ClpX protomer.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on the quality of the cryo-EM maps.

claims.claim: In Conformation A, there is strong density for ATP and a magnesium cofactor in protomers X2, X3, X4, and X5.
claims.source: In Conformation A, there is strong density for ATP and a magnesium cofactor in protomers X2, X3, X4, and X5, while the X1 and X6 protomers are ADP loaded, with no density for either the γ-phosphate or magnesium (Figure 4A and C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 4A and C.

claims.claim: In Conformation A, the X1 and X6 protomers are ADP loaded, with no density for either the γ-phosphate or magnesium.
claims.source: In Conformation A, there is strong density for ATP and a magnesium cofactor in protomers X2, X3, X4, and X5, while the X1 and X6 protomers are ADP loaded, with no density for either the γ-phosphate or magnesium (Figure 4A and C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 4A and C.

claims.claim: The orientation between the large and the small AAA+ domains of ClpX changes considerably depending on the nucleotide state.
claims.source: As in both the classic and HCLR clades of AAA+ ATPases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017), the orientation between the large and the small AAA+ domains of ClpX changes considerably depending on the nucleotide state.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures and is consistent with other AAA+ ATPases.

claims.claim: In Conformation A, both the X1 and X6 protomers adopt conformations that allow the X1 protomer to move away from the pore in the US position.
claims.source: In Conformation A, both the X1 and X6 protomers adopt conformations that allow the X1 protomer to move away from the pore in the US position (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and there is reduced surface area buried between X1 and its neighboring protomers X2 and X6.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The local resolution in the cryo-EM maps suggests that the X1 protomer in the US position is significantly more flexible than the other protomers.
claims.source: In agreement with this finding, the local resolution in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggests that the X1 protomer in the US position is significantly more flexible than the other protomers.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the local resolution maps shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, only the X6 protomer is ADP-bound.
claims.source: In Conformation B, only the X6 protomer is ADP-bound.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, the X1, X2, X3, X4, and X5 protomers are ATP-bound with clear density for the γ-phosphate and the magnesium cofactor.
claims.source: The X1, X2, X3, X4, and X5 protomers are ATP-bound with clear density for the γ-phosphate and the magnesium cofactor (Figure 4B and D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 4B and D.

claims.claim: The X5 protomer adopts a unique orientation between its large domain and small domain compared to the other ATP-bound protomers in order to accommodate the translation of the X6 protomer away from the substrate translocation channel into the LS position.
claims.source: Interestingly, the X5 protomer adopts a unique orientation between its large domain and small domain compared to the other ATP-bound protomers in order to accommodate the translation of the X6 protomer away from the substrate translocation channel into the LS position (Figure 4B orange box; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In Conformation A, the β- and γ-phosphates of the bound ATP are stabilized by interactions with the sensor-II arginine (Arg369) of the same subunit and the arginine finger (Arg306) from the adjacent clockwise protomer.
claims.source: In Conformation A, the β- and γ-phosphates of the bound ATP are stabilized by interactions with the sensor-II arginine (Arg369) of the same subunit and the arginine finger (Arg306) from the adjacent clockwise protomer (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: In the ADP-bound sites of the X1 and X6 protomers in Conformation A, both arginines have moved away, allowing for a more open nucleotide-binding pocket.
claims.source: In the ADP-bound sites of the X1 and X6 protomers, both arginines have moved away, allowing for a more open nucleotide-binding pocket (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: In Conformation B, both the sensor-II arginine and the arginine finger contact the β and γ-phosphates in only four of the five ATP-bound protomers (X1, X2, X3, and X4).
claims.source: In Conformation B, both the sensor-II arginine and the arginine finger contact the β and γ-phosphates in only four of the five ATP-bound protomers (X1, X2, X3, and X4) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In the X5 protomer of Conformation B, the adjacent X6 protomer and its arginine finger have pivoted away from the nucleotide into the LS position, allowing the sensor-II arginine to move closer to the γ-phosphate of the bound nucleotide.
claims.source: In the X5 protomer (at the bottom of the spiral), the adjacent X6 protomer and its arginine finger have pivoted away from the nucleotide into the LS position, allowing the sensor-II arginine to move closer to the γ-phosphate of the bound nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claims.claim: The resolution of the experimental map was not sufficient to differentiate between ATP and a long-lived post-hydrolysis ADP/Pi state in the X5 protomer of Conformation B.
claims.source: While there is clear density for the γ-phosphate, the resolution of our experimental map was not sufficient to differentiate between ATP and a long-lived post-hydrolysis ADP/Pi state.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the resolution of the cryo-EM maps.

claims.claim: The sensor II-priming motif in the nucleotide site adjacent to an ADP bound site has also been reported for the Lon protease bound to substrate.
claims.source: Notably, this key sensor II-priming motif in the nucleotide site adjacent to an ADP bound site has also been reported for the Lon protease bound to substrate (Shin et al., 2019), a close relative in the HCLR clade of AAA+ proteins.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to Shin et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Two distinct conformations of ClpX were identified, at 3.3 Å and 2.9 Å resolution, referred to as Conformations A and B, respectively.
claims.source: Further local refinement and classification in cryoSPARC (Punjani et al., 2017) improved the density for ClpX and revealed two distinct conformations, at 3.3 Å and 2.9 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), hereafter referred to as Conformations A and B, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the image processing workflow.

claims.claim: Focused refinement of ClpP with D7 symmetry enforced led to a map at 2.3 Å resolution.
claims.source: Focused refinement of ClpP with D7 symmetry enforced led to a map at 2.3 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the image processing workflow.

claims.claim: The transition from Conformation A to Conformation B involves X1 moving to the highest position of the spiral with respect to substrate and simultaneously exchanging ADP for ATP in its nucleotide-binding pocket.
claims.source: In Conformation B, X1 moves to the highest position of the spiral with respect to substrate (compare Figure 2F, top and bottom panels) simultaneously exchanging ADP for ATP in its nucleotide-binding pocket (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5B and Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The transition from Conformation A to Conformation B brings X1 into close proximity with X2 and allows engagement of X1's pore loops with substrate.
claims.source: This transition brings X1 into close proximity with X2 and allows engagement of X1's pore loops with substrate.
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion as part of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: The X1 pore-l loop sits at the top of the spiral, two substrate residues above the X2 pore loop in Conformation B.
claims.source: The X1 pore-l loop now sits at the top of the spiral, two substrate residues above the X2 pore loop (Figure 5A and B), thereby translocating additional residues of substrate into the unfoldase.
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: The transition from Conformation A to Conformation B leads to release of substrate by X6, which pivots away from the central pore to adopt the LS position.
claims.source: This transition also leads to release of substrate by X6, which pivots away from the central pore to adopt the LS position (second ring, Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release by X5 restores the ClpX spiral back to the Conformation A state.
claims.source: ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release by X5, which was in the ATP-hydrolysis primed ATP* state, restores the ClpX spiral back to the Conformation A state, (third ring of the four in Figure 5A), with X6 now assuming the US position.
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Each Conformation A→Conformation B→Conformation A step results in the exchange of ADP for ATP and a single ATP hydrolysis event.
claims.source: Each Conformation A→Conformation B→Conformation A step results in the exchange of ADP for ATP and a single ATP hydrolysis event.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Continuous repetition of the A→B→A steps leads to a processive 'hand-over-hand' translocation of substrate through the axial pore of ClpX into ClpP.
claims.source: Continuous repetition of these steps leads to a processive 'hand-over-hand' translocation of substrate through the axial pore of ClpX into ClpP (Illustrated in Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Video 2.

claims.claim: The sequential hydrolysis of ATP results in unidirectional substrate translocation and movement of pore loops along the substrate.
claims.source: The sequential hydrolysis of ATP at the ATP* position results in unidirectional substrate translocation and movement of pore loops along the substrate (Figure 5B), with the counter clockwise hydrolysis cycle translating into a repeated downward pulling force on the substrate.
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Both the sequential hydrolysis of ATP as well as the 'hand-over-hand' substrate pulling model appear to be conserved for AAA+ unfoldases.
claims.source: Both the sequential hydrolysis of ATP as well as the 'hand-over-hand' substrate pulling model appear to be conserved for AAA+ unfoldases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on other AAA+ unfoldases.

claims.claim: Following ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release, the IGF loop of the protomer in the ATP* position must leave its engaged pocket and move to bind the adjacent empty site on ClpP.
claims.source: Thus, following ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release, the IGF loop of the protomer in the ATP* position (X5 initially) must leave its engaged pocket and move to bind the adjacent empty site on ClpP (red arrows in Figure 5C), as the complex transitions back to Conformation A (third ring in Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5C and Figure 5A.

claims.claim: After seven IGF loop release and reengagement events, accompanied by seven ATP hydrolysis steps, the 'empty' ClpP binding site makes a complete cycle, returning to its starting position.
claims.source: After seven IGF loop release and reengagement events, accompanied by seven ATP hydrolysis steps, the 'empty' ClpP binding site makes a complete cycle, returning to its starting position (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Seven IGF loop transitions lead to a net 60° rotation of ClpX with respect to ClpP.
claims.source: The accompanying motion of ClpX on the apical surface of ClpP for a given IGF loop transition is complex and subtle, yet seven of these transitions lead to a net 60° rotation of ClpX with respect to ClpP (note the positions of the purple ClpX protomer in the first and seventh panels in Figure 5D; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5D and Video 3.

claims.claim: The IGF loop of the X5 protomer has an 'extended/stretched' structure in the ATP* position of Conformation B, which likely causes strain and facilitates loop release and subsequent binding to the corresponding site on the adjacent ClpP protomer.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, the IGF loop of the X5 protomer has an 'extended/stretched' structure in the ATP* position of Conformation B (Figure 2F), which likely causes strain and facilitates loop release and subsequent binding to the corresponding site on the adjacent ClpP protomer (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 2F and Figure 5C.

claims.claim: During preparation of this manuscript, two manuscript preprints reported structures of ClpXP from L. monocytogenes and from E. coli.
claims.source: During preparation of this manuscript, two manuscript preprints reported structures of ClpXP from L. monocytogenes (Gatsogiannis et al., 2019) and from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019), with ClpX resolutions ranging from 3.9 to 6 Å.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to the preprints.

claims.claim: In all species, the ClpX ring appears to adopt a similar offset relative to the symmetry axis of ClpP, indicating that the general architecture of the ClpXP machinery is conserved.
claims.source: In all species, the ClpX ring appears to adopt a similar offset relative to the symmetry axis of ClpP, indicating that the general architecture of the ClpXP machinery is conserved.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the NmClpXP structures to those from other species.

claims.claim: The N-terminal apical loops of L. monocytogenes ClpP are not rigidified upon ClpX binding, in contrast to the observation in N. meningitidis that the gates rigidify upon binding.
claims.source: Notably, however, the N-terminal apical loops of L. monocytogenes ClpP are not rigidified upon ClpX binding (Gatsogiannis et al., 2019), in contrast to the observation here that the gates rigidify upon binding to create a pore for substrate entry.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the NmClpXP structures to those from L. monocytogenes.

claims.claim: Unusual head-to-head dimers of L. monocytogenes ClpXP were observed that appeared to be mediated by the zinc binding domains.
claims.source: In the case of L. monocytogenes ClpXP, unusual head-to-head dimers were observed that appeared to be mediated by the zinc binding domains.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to Gatsogiannis et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Despite the presence of the zinc-binding domains in the N. meningitidis construct, no head-to-head dimers were observed.
claims.source: Despite the presence of the zinc-binding domains in our N. meningitidis construct, no such dimers were observed.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claims.claim: The glutaraldehyde chemical crosslinker used to stabilize the L. monocytogenes ClpXP complex may have induced the formation of artefactual dimers.
claims.source: While this difference may be due to differences across species, we note that the glutaraldehyde chemical crosslinker used to stabilize the L. monocytogenes ClpXP complex may have induced the formation of artefactual dimers.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the difference.

claims.claim: Substrate engagement is different between the ClpXP from N. meningitidis and from E. coli.
claims.source: Notably, substrate engagement is different between the ClpXP from N. meningitidis described here and from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the two structures.

claims.claim: In N. meningitidis Conformation A, there is no engagement of substrate by any of the six pore-2 or six RKH loops.
claims.source: In Conformation A seen with N. meningitidis, there is no engagement of substrate by any of the six pore-2 or six RKH loops, while in Conformation B only a single RKH loop and a single pore-2 loop contact substrate (Figure 3D and F).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and F.

claims.claim: In recently reported E. coli ClpXP structures, arginines located in the pore-2 loop from three to five different protomers, as well as multiple RKH loops, form major contacts with substrate.
claims.source: This observation is in contrast to the recently reported E. coli ClpXP structures (Fei et al., 2019) in which arginines located in the pore-2 loop from three to five different protomers (depending on the structure), as well as multiple RKH loops, form major contacts with substrate.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to Fei et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The differences in substrate interactions may reflect that while pore-1 loop and RKH loop motifs are critical for forming interactions with substrate and providing the force for translocation, additional contacts may differ between species and may be necessary for recognition of degradation signals and for substrate specificity.
claims.source: The differences in these interactions may reflect the fact that while pore-1 loop and RKH loop motifs are critical for forming interactions with substrate, and in the case of pore-1 loops in particular, in providing the force for translocation, additional contacts may differ between species and may be necessary for recognition of degradation signals and for substrate specificity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observed differences.

claims.claim: The RKH loops are essential for the recognition of SsrA-tagged substrates by E. coli ClpX.
claims.source: The RKH loops are essential for the recognition of SsrA-tagged substrates by E. coli ClpX, while human ClpX, which substitutes the RKH sequence with an RKL tripeptide and contains pore-1 loops with the same sequence as E. coli ClpX, fails to recognize substrates with the SsrA-tag.
claims.evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claims.claim: An engineered human ClpX construct bearing the pore-2 and RKH loops of E. coli ClpX is able to unfold SsrA-tagged substrates.
claims.source: Notably, however, an engineered human construct bearing the pore-2 and RKH loops of E. coli ClpX is able to unfold SsrA-tagged substrates (Farrell et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to Farrell et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Reordering of RKH loop residues to KHR and KRH results in significantly impaired substrate degradation.
claims.source: Reordering of RKH loop residues to KHR and KRH results in significantly impaired substrate degradation (Fei et al., 2019) and a more disrupting AAA mutant does not support ClpP degradation of a SsrA-tagged substrate (Fei et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to Fei et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The single point mutation RKH to RKA results in loss of activity for both SsrA and λO tagged substrates.
claims.source: Furthermore, the single point mutation RKH to RKA results in loss of activity for both SsrA and λO tagged substrates.
claims.evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claims.claim: The tight contact between H230 and the substrate in the N. meningitidis ClpXP maps provides a structural basis for understanding mutagenesis results showing the importance of the RKH loop.
claims.source: The tight contact between H230 and the substrate in our maps provides a structural basis for understanding these mutagenesis results.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural data in light of previous mutagenesis studies.

claims.claim: In the ClpXP structures from E. coli, the ClpX ring adopts the same spiral staircase arrangement observed in many AAA+ ATPases, strongly supporting the 'hand-over-hand' mechanism of substrate translocation.
claims.source: Although in the ClpXP structures from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019) the ClpX ring adopts the same spiral staircase arrangement observed in many AAA+ ATPases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Huang et al., 2016), strongly supporting the 'hand-over-hand' mechanism of substrate translocation, the authors of this work instead posit a stochastic mechanism (Fei et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2005) for the HCLR clade of ATPases based on the observation of only a single bound ADP in their structures.
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to the E. coli ClpXP structures and other AAA+ ATPases.

claims.claim: The authors of the E. coli ClpXP work posit a stochastic mechanism for the HCLR clade of ATPases based on the observation of only a single bound ADP in their structures.
claims.source: Although in the ClpXP structures from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019) the ClpX ring adopts the same spiral staircase arrangement observed in many AAA+ ATPases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Huang et al., 2016), strongly supporting the 'hand-over-hand' mechanism of substrate translocation, the authors of this work instead posit a stochastic mechanism (Fei et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2005) for the HCLR clade of ATPases based on the observation of only a single bound ADP in their structures.

claims.claim: A stochastic model involving stochastic nucleotide hydrolysis appears inconsistent with the observations in N. meningitidis ClpXP, with those for the related Lon protease where two neighboring protomers are bound with ADP, and with a recent structural model for a substrate-bound E. coli ClpAP complex.

results.result: Cryo-EM structures of substrate-bound N. meningitidis ClpXP were determined at high resolution. Two distinct conformations of ClpX (Conformations A and B) were resolved at 3.3 Å and 2.9 Å respectively, while ClpP was refined to 2.3 Å with D7 symmetry.
results.evaluation: The resolution values are explicitly stated and supported by FSC curves, orientation distributions, and model statistics in Table 1. The image processing workflow is clearly documented showing the separation of two conformations through 3D variability analysis and heterogeneous classification. The quality metrics (MolProbity scores, EMRinger, map-model correlation) validate the structural models.

results.result: The overall architecture of ClpXP shows a hexameric ClpX ring positioned with an offset and tilt relative to the seven-fold symmetric ClpP tetradecamer, yet maintaining a continuous channel for substrate. ClpP adopts its active extended conformation closely resembling ADEP-bound structures.
results.evaluation: The structural composition is directly observed in the cryo-EM maps and models. The offset and tilt are clearly visible in Figures 1D-F and Video 1. The RMSD comparison to ADEP-bound ClpP (1.18 Å) provides quantitative validation. The continuous channel is evident in the density maps.

results.result: Functional ClpXP complexes from N. meningitidis were reconstituted in vitro and shown to degrade GFP-SsrA in an ATP-dependent manner. An E185Q Walker B mutant was used to slow ATP hydrolysis and stabilize the complex for structural studies, forming singly and doubly capped complexes observable by SEC.
results.evaluation: The degradation assays (Figure 1B) clearly demonstrate ATP-dependence with appropriate controls. SEC data (Figure 1C) with SDS-PAGE confirmation shows complex formation. The use of the Walker B mutant is a standard approach for stabilizing AAA+ ATPases, though this does limit interpretation of the native catalytic cycle.

results.result: In both conformations, substrate enters ClpX at ~15° relative to ClpP's symmetry axis and is gripped by five of six protomers arranged in a right-handed spiral, with Tyr153 of pore-1 loops forming the primary interface. The sixth protomer forms a disengaged 'seam' that occupies different positions: 'upper seam' (US) in Conformation A (protomer X1) and 'lower seam' (LS) in Conformation B (protomer X6).
results.evaluation: The spiral arrangement and substrate engagement are clearly visible in the cryo-EM density (Figures 1F, 3A-D). The angle measurement and identification of Tyr153 contacts are directly observable. The distinction between US and LS positions is well-documented structurally. This is consistent with other AAA+ ATPases as noted by the authors.

results.result: IGF loops from ClpX bind to hydrophobic pockets on ClpP with variable occupancy and flexibility. In Conformation A, only five IGF loops show clear density, while in Conformation B all six are resolved. The empty ClpP-binding pocket is consistently located between X5 and X6 protomers. The flexibility of IGF loops and adjacent residues (275-280) accommodates the spiral arrangement of ClpX while maintaining contact with planar ClpP.
results.evaluation: The density for IGF loops is clearly shown in Figures 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The variable density is appropriately interpreted as flexibility and sub-stoichiometric binding. The structural observation that IGF loops adopt different configurations in the two conformations supports their proposed role as flexible tethers.

results.result: ClpX binding induces ordering of ClpP N-terminal gates into β-hairpins, creating a ~23 Å entrance pore. This represents a disorder-to-order transition similar to ADEP binding. Gate rigidification varies between protomers, with the X5 protomer uniquely contacting one gate through three α-helices that stabilize the β-hairpin via Arg17 interactions. Most gate rigidification appears mediated by allosteric effects from IGF loop binding.
results.evaluation: The ordered β-hairpins are clearly visible in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and contrast with disordered gates in apo-ClpP. The pore diameter measurement is straightforward. The comparison to ADEP-bound structures is validated by structural similarity. The specific X5-gate contacts are well-resolved. The allosteric interpretation is reasonable given that most gates are rigidified without direct ClpX contact.

results.result: Substrate engagement involves primarily pore-1 loops in both conformations, with additional contacts from pore-2 and RKH loops in Conformation B. The X1 pore-2 loop (Ile198, Thr199) and X5 RKH loop (His230) engage substrate in Conformation B. The X6 pore-1 loop undergoes a large conformational change upon disengagement, transitioning from a 'lasso' fold to an α-helix.
results.evaluation: The substrate-loop contacts are clearly resolved in the 2.9-3.3 Å maps (Figures 3A-F). The conformational change of the X6 pore-1 loop is well-documented (Figure 3E). The identification of specific residues making substrate contacts is appropriate at this resolution. The observation that most RKH loops are flexible and not contacting substrate is supported by weak density.

results.result: Nucleotide states were unambiguously identified in each protomer. Conformation A has ATP in X2-X5 and ADP in X1 and X6. Conformation B has ATP in X1-X5 and ADP only in X6. In ATP-bound sites, sensor-II arginine (R369) and arginine finger (R306) stabilize β- and γ-phosphates, except in the X5 protomer of Conformation B where only sensor-II contacts the nucleotide (ATP* state). The resolution was insufficient to distinguish ATP from ADP·Pi in X5.
results.evaluation: The nucleotide density is clearly shown in Figures 4A-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3. The identification of ATP vs ADP based on γ-phosphate density is appropriate at 2.9-3.3 Å resolution. The arginine positions are well-resolved. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation in distinguishing ATP from ADP·Pi in the X5 site. The ATP* designation is consistent with observations in related Lon protease.

results.result: The orientation between large and small AAA+ domains changes with nucleotide state. In Conformation A, ADP-bound X1 and X6 adopt conformations allowing X1 to move away from the pore (US position) with reduced buried surface area and increased flexibility. In Conformation B, X5 adopts a unique domain orientation to accommodate X6 translation to the LS position.
results.evaluation: The domain reorientations are clearly visible in the structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The local resolution maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) support increased flexibility of X1 in the US position. These observations are consistent with nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in other AAA+ ATPases.

results.result: A mechanistic model proposes that sequential ATP hydrolysis drives a processive hand-over-hand translocation mechanism. The A→B transition involves X1 exchanging ADP for ATP, moving to the top of the spiral, and engaging substrate while X6 disengages. The B→A transition involves ATP hydrolysis by X5 (ATP* state), returning the spiral to Conformation A with X6 in the US position. Each cycle translocates substrate by ~2 residues with one ATP hydrolysis event.
results.evaluation: While the two conformations are well-resolved and the structural differences clearly documented, the proposed mechanism involves significant inference beyond the static structures. The model assumes these two conformations represent sequential steps in a cycle, but the structures are from a Walker B mutant with impaired hydrolysis. The directionality and order of transitions are inferred rather than directly observed. Time-resolved or additional intermediate structures would strengthen this mechanistic model. The model is plausible and consistent with the data, but represents a hypothesis requiring further validation.

results.result: IGF loop dynamics are proposed to couple ATP hydrolysis to ClpX rotation on ClpP. Following ATP hydrolysis at the ATP* position, the IGF loop must release and rebind to the adjacent empty ClpP pocket. Seven such transitions complete one cycle of the empty pocket around ClpP, resulting in a net 60° rotation of ClpX relative to ClpP. The extended/stretched structure of the X5 IGF loop in the ATP* state may facilitate this release.
results.evaluation: The structural observation of the extended X5 IGF loop in Conformation B is well-supported (Figure 2F). However, the proposed mechanism of IGF loop release and rebinding is inferred from comparing the two static structures. The calculation that seven transitions lead to 60° rotation is geometrically sound given the 6:7 symmetry mismatch. The model is logical and consistent with the structures, but the dynamic process of loop release and rebinding is not directly observed. Additional evidence (e.g., mutagenesis, time-resolved studies) would be needed to confirm this mechanism.

results.result: The ClpXP translocation mechanism fits the emerging consensus for AAA+ unfoldases, with both sequential ATP hydrolysis and hand-over-hand substrate pulling appearing to be conserved features. The translocating forces generated by AAA+ molecular machines likely operate by a common mechanism despite unique functional features.
results.evaluation: The structural similarity to other AAA+ ATPases (spiral arrangement, pore loop engagement) is well-documented with appropriate citations. The comparison is valid and the conclusion that ClpXP uses a similar mechanism is reasonable. However, this is a comparative/interpretive conclusion rather than a direct experimental result. The statement about a 'common mechanism' is appropriately qualified as 'likely' and acknowledges that unique features will continue to emerge.

results.result: Comparison with ClpXP structures from other species reveals conserved overall architecture but species-specific differences. The ClpX offset relative to ClpP is conserved across species. However, N. meningitidis shows rigidified ClpP gates upon ClpX binding (unlike L. monocytogenes), no head-to-head dimers (unlike L. monocytogenes), and different substrate engagement patterns compared to E. coli (minimal pore-2/RKH loop contacts in N. meningitidis vs. extensive contacts in E. coli).
results.evaluation: The comparisons are appropriately qualified given that the other structures are at lower resolution (3.9-6 Å) and detailed maps/models were not available. The observation about gate rigidification is a clear difference. The suggestion that glutaraldehyde crosslinking may have caused artifactual dimers in L. monocytogenes is reasonable speculation. The differences in substrate engagement are clearly documented (Figures 3D, F vs. cited E. coli structures). The interpretation that these differences may relate to substrate specificity is plausible but speculative.

results.result: The structural observation of His230 (RKH loop) contacting substrate in N. meningitidis ClpXP provides a structural basis for understanding mutagenesis studies showing the importance of RKH loops for SsrA-tagged substrate recognition and degradation in E. coli ClpX.
results.evaluation: The contact between His230 and substrate is clearly resolved in the structures (Figures 3D, F). The cited mutagenesis studies from other groups provide independent validation of RKH loop importance. The structural data nicely explain the functional data, though the studies are from different species. This represents a good integration of structural and functional data.

results.result: The authors argue against a stochastic mechanism proposed for E. coli ClpXP, noting that their observation of two neighboring ADP-bound protomers in Conformation A is inconsistent with stochastic hydrolysis and instead supports sequential hydrolysis, similar to the mechanism proposed for E. coli ClpAP and Lon protease.
results.evaluation: The observation of two ADP-bound protomers (X1 and X6) in Conformation A is clearly documented in the structures. This is indeed inconsistent with a strictly stochastic model where only one ADP would be expected. The comparison to Lon protease (also showing two neighboring ADPs) and ClpAP provides supporting evidence. However, this is a rebuttal argument based on structural snapshots from a Walker B mutant, so some caution is warranted. The argument is logical and well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: ClpXP functions to unfold, translocate, and degrade protein substrates using energy from ATP hydrolysis. Bulky aromatic and aliphatic side chains of pore loops transmit pulling force to the substrate.
results.evaluation: These are well-established functions of ClpXP supported by extensive prior literature and confirmed by the degradation assays in this study. The structural data showing pore loop-substrate contacts (particularly Tyr153) directly support the mechanism of force transmission. This is background knowledge validated by the current structural results.

results.result: ClpXP is an important drug target for infectious diseases and cancer, with its function being critical in bacteria and mitochondria. Small molecule inhibitors targeting ClpP, ClpX, or their interaction can kill cells.
results.evaluation: These claims are well-supported by the extensive citations provided. This represents established knowledge in the field that provides motivation for the structural studies. The authors appropriately cite primary literature for each class of inhibitors and therapeutic applications.

results.result: Prior structural and biochemical studies established the basic architecture and functional elements of ClpXP, including ClpP's barrel structure with catalytic triads, ClpX binding via IGF loops, gated entry to the degradation chamber, and the roles of RKH and pore loops. However, structures of substrate-bound ClpXP holoenzyme were lacking, preventing understanding of the conformational changes during substrate processing and how the 6:7 symmetry mismatch is accommodated.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize prior knowledge with appropriate citations. The authors correctly identify the gap in knowledge (lack of substrate-bound holoenzyme structures) that their work addresses. This provides proper context for the significance of the current study.
